column1: # Ordering is real corpus frequency, not a hand-guessed list: the English side
# is the top of the OpenSubtitles 2018 English frequency list
# (github.com/hermitdave/FrequencyWords), reduced to one entry per lemma using
# the extension's own lemmatizer, so "is", "are" and "was" arrive as a single
# "be" entry that every form on a page can reach.
# Also removed: contraction fragments left behind when apostrophes are stripped
# ("don", "didn"), transcription fillers ("uh", "hmm"), proper nouns, and six
# profanities that are genuinely frequent in subtitles but a surprising default
# to swap into someone's web pages.
# The file ends with a phrase section (Phase 3). Those entries are multi-word,
# and `token_count` is derived from them on import, which is what tells the
# extension how far to walk its n-gram pass.
# Their ranks are the one hand-placed thing in this file. The corpus list is
# unigrams, so it cannot say where "of course" belongs among single words; the
# ranks below are an estimate of where these phrases would fall if it could,
# and they are interleaved with the words rather than appended after them so a
# learner actually reaches a phrase before exhausting 494 single words. Replace
# them the day a bigram frequency list is wired into build_dictionary.py.
# Multi-word entries. The extension matches the longest one that fits, so
# "a lot of" wins over the "a" entry that starts in the same place, and it
# lemmatizes only the head: "gave up" and "gives up" both reach "give up",
# which is where English phrases carry their inflection.
# The target side is still one base form, as it is for single words — "give up"
# is "rendirse", never "se rindió". Phase 4 is what fixes that.
